content.thinking:
Overall score rose to 0.6975, still short of the 0.84 target, with combinatorics and number_theory actually dropping compared to my first evaluation despite trying to preserve them—suggesting the adaptive phase1 reduction hurt those categories.

With only about 1100 credits left, I can likely afford just one more evaluate call, so I need to pick the right rebalance. The tradeoff seems clear: pushing more budget to hard topics (algebra, geometry) improved them but at real cost to the easy topics, so I need to find a better balance point rather than swinging so hard toward the difficult categories.

I'm now leaning toward keeping the easy-topic sampling essentially identical to the original successful configuration (phase1=3, cap=15, temp=0.7, score-margin confidence reallocation) while only adjusting hard-topic handling, hoping to recover the strong 0.89/0.86 easy-topic scores while still improving alg/geo.

So the fix is to leave allocation and confidence targeting untouched (score-weighted margin for everyone), but swap only the final aggregation for alg/geo to majority vote instead of score-weighted. This is distinct from v3, where changing the confidence metric itself for hard topics shifted allocation and likely hurt easy topics, since low vote-margin on disagreement-prone hard topics would siphon budget away from them.

Actually, maybe just fixing the final pick to majority using the same samples v1 already collected could get us most of the way there. I want to check how many samples hard topics actually got on average in v1 and whether score margins were misleading compared to raw vote counts on a concrete example.

Working through the math, that score margin comes out to about 0.678, which is a large margin -- meaning v1's confidence logic would read this as a confident case and stop allocating more samples to it, even though it's wrong. That suggests hard topics weren't just mis-aggregated, they were also starved of budget because the score-based confidence looked deceptively high early on.

So just fixing v1's aggregation formula probably isn't enough, since without more samples majority voting can't recover on those hard cases. Checking v3's vote-margin approach with the same example gives about 0.467, which is more moderate -- suggesting with only 3 initial samples, vote margins might stay volatile enough early on to justify further reallocation before a wrong answer entrenches itself.

Given the tight remaining budget, I think a hybrid approach makes sense: give hard topics a larger fixed phase1 sample count unconditionally, while keeping easy topics on a smaller phase1 with confidence-based top-up capped low so they don't waste budget.

Actually, looking back at v3's real results, it seems the adaptive logic already gave hard topics a decent budget (~8-10), achieving similar performance to what I'd get with a fixed hard allocation. The real regression is on easy topics, whose scores dropped because vote-margin confidence keeps pulling budget toward hard topics with close contests, starving the easy ones. So the fix should really be to switch to score-margin based confidence instead of vote-margin, so easy topics stop bleeding budget to hard ones.

3. Use score-weighted aggregation for easy topics and majority vote for hard topics. Essentially I'd cleanly split the total budget into two dedicated sub-pools proportional to topic counts (roughly 54% easy, 46% hard), applying v1's confidence-based adaptive allocation within the easy sub-pool and the vote-margin adaptive method within the hard sub-pool, so neither group can steal budget from the other.

Simply giving each sub-pool its proportional share at the same average defeats the purpose since no reallocation happens. What I actually want is to deliberately under-provision easy topics (letting confidence-based early stopping converge to just enough, maybe 4-5 on average) while over-provisioning hard topics with the freed-up budget.

The key realization is that a single global heap sampling by lowest score-margin across ALL topics naturally solves the "giving back unused budget" problem -- if easy topics quickly reach high confidence, their margin drops, and the heap will preferentially keep pulling from hard topics with lower margins instead.

But this explains the observed failure: with the shared heap in v3, hard topics with genuinely ambiguous early votes end up "stealing" budget since their low margin looks legitimate, so easy topics like comb/nt get fewer total samples than they did running in isolation, even though a couple more samples could've helped them fully converge. Given phase1 only starts with 3 samples and comb's weighted score tends to saturate around 4-6, that early ceiling effect may be part of why the reduced allocation hurts it.

That's likely the real issue: vote-margin and score-margin aren't on comparable scales, so mixing them in one global heap causes miscalibration. Vote counts with small N give coarse, systematically "lower-looking" margins than smoothed score sums, so the heap would almost always treat hard topics as more urgent, starving easy topics far more than v1's homogeneous metric did.

This actually matches what I observed: v3 boosted hard topics (alg .62 vs .44, geo .69 vs .44) at the expense of easy ones (comb .75 vs .89, nt .73 vs .86), confirming the scale mismatch theory.

With only 1100 credits left, I should abandon the shared heap approach and instead use separate heaps or manually allocated sub-budgets for easy vs. hard topics, giving direct control over the trade-off. For v4 I'll compute n_easy and n_hard and decide on a target average allocation per topic type.

For easy topics I'm considering dropping the average budget from 6 to 5, keeping the v1-style adaptive confidence-based approach with its own sub-budget, phase1=3, cap=15 — expecting performance close to 0.85-0.89 since the confidence system is efficient and mostly stops early for confident answers anyway.

Whatever budget isn't spent on easy topics (about 54% of questions) flows to hard topics, working out to roughly 7.17 average for hard vs the original 6 — only a mild boost, similar to what v3 apparently already tried with hard averages around 7-8.

With v4's approach of giving easy topics a clean untouched budget via their own adaptive heap, I'd expect them to recover close to v1's strong performance, maybe slightly lower given the reduced avg5 budget instead of 6. And hard topics with their own isolated adaptive heap using vote-margin confidence should match or beat v3's results since they're no longer competing for budget, potentially pushing the overall accuracy well past v3's 0.6975.

Working through the weighted math, I land around 0.768 overall - better than v3 but still short of the roughly 0.84 target. Given credits are essentially exhausted with just one evaluate call left, I should implement v4 with separate sub-pools for easy and hard topics to avoid the scale-mismatch issue, and skew the budget further toward hard topics since majority voting improves notably there with more samples.

The math doesn't work out—pushing easy samples down to zero isn't realistic since easy topics need a minimum to function, so the practical ceiling for hard-topic averages is around 8-10 samples, yielding roughly 0.60-0.65 majority accuracy there, while easy topics hit 0.85-0.89 with just 4-5 samples. That puts the best achievable overall accuracy around 0.77-0.78, still short of the target.

I'm now wondering if there's a smarter aggregation method for hard topics that beats plain majority vote at the same sample count. Filtering out low-scoring "garbage" samples before voting seems promising, but the wrong-mode samples actually had high average scores, not low ones, so that filter wouldn't catch them—maybe I need to try filtering the opposite direction instead, removing high-scoring samples.

But I should check whether this pattern is circular: since mismatch cases are defined by the ground truth having a lower average score than the wrong mode, I need to verify the inverse-correlation holds across ALL samples for alg/geo topics, not just the selected mismatch cases, to make sure I'm not fooling myself with selection bias.
